attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his authored post.

semantics.note: The proposition accurately restates the claim that one Opus 4.7 request counts as 7.5 premium requests under the April promotion.

contract.note: Reading 'request' as premium-request units per user prompt fits the surrounding multiplier discussion. Using April 2026 as the target period is fair.

evidence.note: GitHub's April 16 changelog announces a 7.5x promotional multiplier until April 30. GitHub is the authority on its own billing rules. The May editor's note added later does not affect the April rate.
The April 17 docs snapshot says Chat uses one premium request per user prompt, multiplied by the model's rate. That gives 7.5 units per Opus 4.7 prompt.

reviews.rationale: GitHub's own April records set a 7.5x promotional multiplier and charge one premium request per prompt times that rate. So each Opus 4.7 prompt counted as 7.5 premium requests, as Zitron said.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytical sentence in his authored post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the named companies, the universal 'every other AI company', and the tokens-versus-subscription comparison.

contract.note: The contract chose March 2026 as the period, and it requires an accounting basis the speaker never gave. Neither choice is decisive here: the packet has no comparable cost data either way.

evidence.note: A blog argument that retail API prices overstate Anthropic's real serving cost. It is an estimate, not provider cost records, and covers only Anthropic. It neither proves nor disproves the claim.
Cursor's July 2025 pricing post. It is from a different period and says nothing about actual compute costs against subscription fees.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no provider cost records comparing compute cost with subscription fees for the named companies, and nothing covering every other AI company. The items are context only. Whether retail API value or actual serving cost is meant remains unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words and arithmetic in his authored post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the promotional-pricing qualifier and the Opus 4.6 baseline. It leaves out the stated baseline multiplier of 3, which the contract checks separately.

contract.note: Reading '250% more' as a 250% increase over the baseline is the ordinary meaning, so this is a fair plain reading. Under it, 7.5 against 3 is a 150% increase.

evidence.note: GitHub's April 17 data file lists standard Opus 4.6 at 3 and Opus 4.7 at 7.5. That is 150% more (250% of the old rate), not 250% more. The baseline of 3 is correct.
The April 17 snapshot confirms that 7.5x was the promotional rate until April 30.

reviews.rationale: The baseline multiplier of 3 for standard Opus 4.6 is correct. But 7.5 against 3 is a 150% increase; 250% is the new rate as a share of the old one. Under the ordinary meaning of 'more', the claimed 250% increase is wrong.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytical sentence in his authored post.

semantics.note: The causal core is that model-running costs drove the billing change. 'Significant move' is evaluative. 'Any AI product' generalizes the claim, possibly as rhetoric.

contract.note: Whether 'any AI product' is a literal universal or rhetoric decides whether evidence about Copilot alone could support the claim. Treating 'reflecting' as a contributing cause is fair.

evidence.note: An April 27 report quotes GitHub's Rodriguez saying escalating inference costs made premium requests unsustainable. This is the company's stated rationale for Copilot only. It does not show costs across AI products.

reviews.rationale: GitHub's own stated rationale backs a cost motive for Copilot's billing change. But that is a company disclosure, and no evidence covers the claimed scope of any AI product. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.
